conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: SurrogateMovingAverageFinerTimeframe
candidates.quote: You actually need to plot a 90 bar moving average on the 1 minute chart as a surrogate for the 5 minute 20 bar moving average... use a 90 bar moving average... which is very close to the 5 minute 20 bar moving average.
candidates.description: If the strategy's bar series is the finer of two nested timeframes (e.g. 1 minute standing in for 5 minute), use an EMA length equal to the coarser timeframe's EMA length times the timeframe ratio, minus a small correction (90 rather than 100 for a 5x ratio and a 20-bar EMA), then take a with-trend high1/low1 or high2/low2 setup at that average, risking only the height of the (smaller) signal bar.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] <= surrogateMovingAverage[0] + toleranceTicks * tickSize && close[0] > open[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the high of the moving-average-touch signal bar

complexity.reason: an EMA maintained bar to bar with a specific length correction, combined with an existing moving-average-touch/high1-2 entry primitive

notes: This only requires a single bar series at the finer resolution (1 minute) with a differently-sized EMA - it does not require the engine to hold two simultaneous timeframes at once.
surrogateEmaLength = 90 is Brooks's specific correction for a 5x ratio and a 20-bar EMA (not simply 5x20=100); the general formula would need re-deriving for other ratios.

candidates.name: TrendLineBreakTestReversalEntry
candidates.quote: After a strong trend line break, look to enter countertrend on a test, like a higher low or lower low in a possible new bull trend, if there is a strong reversal bar.
candidates.description: After a trend line break, enter countertrend on the subsequent test of the trend's prior extreme (a higher low forming in what may be a new bull trend), provided the test bar is a strong reversal bar.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the strong reversal (test) bar's high

complexity.reason: requires trend-line detection/projection from pivots in addition to a swing-low test and a reversal-bar-shape primitive

notes: Composes the trend-line-break primitive and the BullReversalBarShape-style primitive, both defined in earlier chapters; not redefined here.

candidates.name: PostVolatilitySpikeEntryDelay
candidates.quote: In the seconds to minutes after a report comes out, computerized trading by institutions gives them a clear edge in speed of analysis and order placement. When your competition has a big advantage, don't compete. Wait for their edge to disappear... which is usually after the first one to three bars.
candidates.description: After a burst of large-range/outside bars signals an emotional volatility spike (a proxy for a news report, detectable from price alone), wait waitBars bars before taking new entries, letting the initial speed-driven moves fade.

complexity.reason: composes a bar-range-vs-average volatility-spike detector with a bars-since counter

notes: Uses a detectable price-action proxy (a big/outside bar burst) instead of an actual news calendar, unlike the same idea in Chapter 11 which was rejected for needing a report schedule.

candidates.name: FailedNewHighGapTestShort
candidates.quote: Bar 3 was a short on a failed breakout to a new high on a gap up day that could have led to a test of the gap (the market usually tries to test gaps, so traders should look for opportunities to trade in that direction).
candidates.description: On a gap-up session, a failed breakout to a new intraday high is a short signal, since the market usually tries to test back to the gap (the prior close / session open) afterward.
candidates.pseudocode: isGapUpSession && high[0] >= highest(high, n)[1] && close[0] < high[0] - toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop one tick below the failed-breakout bar's low

complexity.reason: combines a session-gap detector, a failed-breakout test (window loop plus close comparison), and an implied gap-test target

notes: The general 'market usually tries to test gaps' tendency is a separate, likely-already-defined gap primitive (see the book's later gap-openings chapter); not redefined here, just composed.

rejected.quote: It is also possible that the daily chart is bearish and the monthly chart is bullish, both at the same time. It is too confusing to try to reconcile all of this... Just pick one time frame, and trade the price action that is in front of you.
rejected.reason: meta-guidance against reconciling multiple timeframes rather than a positive bar-level condition; consistent with the engine already operating on one bar series

rejected.quote: Many traders use charts where the bars are based on volume and not time... You can experiment with totally random numbers of ticks, shares, or minutes per bar and you will see that the charts look great
rejected.reason: bar-construction/infrastructure choice (tick, volume, or time bars), not a trading condition

rejected.quote: There is also a tendency for traders who use charts based on ticks or volume to use smaller time frame charts. They do so to minimize their stop sizes... Invariably, they ignore the trade-off of a lower winning percentage and end up losing money.
rejected.reason: discretionary trader-behavior/personality observation, no bar-level test

rejected.quote: As your position size increases, at some point the volume will affect the market on too many trades on a 1 minute chart. As an extreme example, if you had a profit-target limit order to sell 5,000 Emini contracts at two ticks above the market, anyone with a price ladder would see the aberration
rejected.reason: market-microstructure/execution-slippage consideration tied to the trader's own order size, not a bar-level OHLCV condition

chapter_summary: Chapter 13 is mostly a discussion of which chart timeframe and bar-construction method to trade (5 vs. 1/3 minute, bar vs. candle, time vs. tick vs. volume bars), concluding that price action patterns are the same on any chart and that traders should pick one and master it rather than chase more trades on faster charts. The few mechanizable ideas are: using a length-corrected EMA (90 vs. a naive 100) when trading a finer bar series as a surrogate for a coarser one's moving average, trend-line-break-then-test countertrend entries, delaying entries for a bar or two after a detectable volatility spike (a price-based proxy for 'wait out the news reaction'), and fading a failed new-high breakout on a gap-up day expecting a gap test. Figure 13.7's long bar-by-bar walkthrough is entirely worked examples of primitives already mined elsewhere (high1/2, low2, wedge, double top, moving-average setups, second entries, trend-channel-line reversals) and did not yield new candidates.
